Market Hall: the holder's Tithe can go a point higher per tier.
Market Hall: anyone listing at a board in its town may hold a quarter more listings per tier.
Shrine: each tier gives its holder +1 Standing every week.
Shrine: it also gives 50 influence a tier for every gate felled in the seat's region that week.
Watchtowers: members are told when a challenger reaches half (tier 1) or a quarter (tier 2) of their defence.
Crafting Halls: members crafting in the seat's town get a quality step per tier of Forge and Workshop.
Harbour: a coastal seat can raise a Harbour, making the town a port for the holder's members.
Siegewright: Carpentry's master choice is open now; a work it begins stands a day sooner.
Ram Kit: made at Carpentry 60 from 40 Oak Planks, 20 Iron Ingots and 4 Bear Hides.
Ram Kit: it goes to your Stores and never to your pack.
Gatehouse: it stands at the Throne with 20,000 health, half again for each tier.
Gatehouse: a crown always has one; a palace gains one once its holder raises it.
Rams: Ram Kits become Rams at the gate one at a time, each with 3,000 health (4,500 with a Siegewright).
Walls: each tier brings the defenders back 3 seconds sooner after they fall.
Siege Bar: it shows Gatehouse and Ram health, the Ram's next stroke, Rams in camp and the Walls' tier.
Barracks: a seat's Barracks sends 2, 4 or 6 town guards to fight for the holder, each at a post.
Revolts: a seat whose Standing falls to 0 at the Turning revolts in the holder's siege window the next week.
Revolts: a Rebel Captain (400 health) and 12 rebels hold the palace door and attack nearby fighters.
Revolts: the holder's members have two hours to fell the Captain; if they do, Standing returns to 20.
Revolts: if he still stands or nobody comes, the Charter lapses.
Revolts: a revolt earns no Honours.
Siege Bar: it shows the Captain's health and rebels standing, and the Chronicle records the ending.
Palace Hall: a palace seat's holder has that palace as a guild hall.
Palace Hall: members can open the guild's Stores from any cupboard there and rest in its beds.
Charter Room: the holder's Officers and guildmaster can decorate the palace's largest room with up to 100 pieces.
Charter Room: a board placed there is the guild's own board, as in a guild hall.
Charter Room: no piece can stand within 2 m of anyone in the palace or of a quest's spot.
Charter Room: when the seat changes hands or its Charter lapses, everything in it goes with no refund.
Crown Castle: a crown-holder's castle throne room is its hall, with the guild's banners behind the throne.
Battle: you can now leave a siege or Royal Tourney with Leave, Close, /leave, walking out, or dying.
Battle: each battle at a seat is announced in red at the Turning, a day, an hour, five minutes before.
Siege: arrows, harmful spells and heals now count; Teleport, Recall and Levitate don't work in a siege.
Siege: spectators get a free camera while they watch and no longer stand on the field.
Siege: a dropped fighter's place is held for five minutes; back in time, you return at your side's camp.
Fealty and Pacts: an offer made to your guild can now be declined from the Seat tab.
Chronicle: it now says how long a captured seat's siege lasted and what Conscription and fealty paid.
Hall of Records: it can be read from every seat's board and the three crown castles' shelves.
Siege: a battle nobody finished is void at the Turning; Sellswords' fees go home and the challenger keeps its Right.
Seats: a seat struck from the registry returns its holder's claim fee, if the Charter was won this Season.
Seasons: a Charter won at Season 1's first Turning now counts as held for the whole Season.
The Tithe: a split sale is now taxed on the whole sale, as the market tax is.
Seat Tab: it reloads after every act, and the Relinquish button resets after four seconds.
Market Hall: the extra Tithe points it gives can now be set at the board.
Revolts: a revolt's defenders no longer need to have contributed to the guild the week before.
Gatehouse: a crown's Gatehouse stands from the start, and the Seat tab shows it.
Edicts: the Bounty Edict's words now say "near the town".
Apothecary: it can't be raised until the professions it serves are in.
Tides: the Daedric Incursion's words now say gate kills give double silver too.
Fortifications: a project whose day had come now counts when its seat is captured; works drop from that tier.
The Tithe: a crown's Tithe can now be set above 15% with a Market Hall, instead of failing.
Seasons: a Season's end now lowers a project under way with its work; materials return to the stockpile.
Fortifications: a Charter lost now stops its works' projects; materials return to the stockpile.
Seat Writs: they can only be delivered while the guild holds the seat or is pledged there.
Siege: guards, rebels and the Rebel Captain can't be shot from beyond their reach; one struck comes for you.
Palace Hall: loading into a palace or crown castle now finds its guild hall.
Siege: a fallen guard or rebel no longer replays its fall every second.
Siege Bar: it is hidden when you die or another window takes your seat.
Charter Room: a chest pressed by a visitor now says whose it is.
Siege: siege and Royal Tourney results now reach the server; receipts were checked against the wrong account id.
Edicts: an Edict changed during the Turning could pay out more than set aside; it now settles again.
Siege: a fighter can no longer climb above the field or sink under it; a Tourney bout needs both level.
Siege: a fighter who reconnects returns to their side's camp straight away.
Royal Tourney: the Tourney's 48 now counts a returning contender too.
Siege Receipt: it can be collected as soon as a battle ends, even if your place was taken while away.
Honours: they go to the character who signed for the battle.
Upkeep: a crown's upkeep shown in the Seat tab now uses the same week the Turning uses.
Market Hall: its extra listings can now be used from the market tab, and listing hints include the Tithe.
The Tithe: a Tithe above its cap after a Season's wear lowers the Market Hall comes down with it.
Pledges: five regions now counts the regions your guild holds as well as those it pledged.
Seat Tab: a crown's Seat tab shows its Saturday siege slot instead of the holder's window.
Palace Hall: a palace hall lost while you're inside no longer leaves its furniture in your save.
Seats: they are read again a minute after a failed read, instead of waiting until you travel.
Titles: changing your aura, buying an insignia or unlinking Patreon no longer hides a Charter's title.
Curfew: the night watch comes out at the sky's night.
Pacts: pact breaks are limited per guild, and the day's red announcements are capped at 20.
Seat Registry: each client works out the seats from its own game files and reports a seat daily.
Fair Sieges: the server keeps every fighter's health and checks every blow, spell and step.
Guild Hall: a guildmaster can buy any house as the guild's hall with Buy it for your guild.
Guild Hall: the treasury pays the house's price plus half again; only gold realm characters put in counts.
Guild Hall: a guild has one hall, which belongs to the guild, not any character.
Guild Hall: the guildmaster and Officers choose whether members or anyone may walk in.
Guild Hall: every cupboard is the guild's chest, opening the guild Stores for members.
Guild Hall: members may rest in its beds, use its crafting stations and cast spells in it.
Guild Hall: Officers decorate it from the catalogue; half a removed piece's cost goes to the treasury.
Guild Hall: your own items can't be placed in a hall, and nothing dropped there stays.
Guild Hall: selling it returns 85% of its cost plus half of what its pieces cost to the treasury.
Guild Hall: a guild with a hall can't be disbanded until the hall is sold.
Guild Hall: the treasury ledger now shows what the hall's gold was for.
Guild Board: every Notice Board has a Guilds tab showing your guild's own board, readable only by members.
Guild Board: any member can pin a note for the guild; you can have 3 up at a time.
Guild Board: you can take down your own notes; the guildmaster and Officers can take down anyone's.
Guild Board: the Guilds tab also shows the guilds recruiting in that town, each under its banner.
Guild Board: Officers can place a Notice Board in the guild's hall that opens the guild's board.
Homes: a new Who may enter setting, My guild, lets members of your character's guild walk in.
Heraldry: every guild can raise a banner of field colour, border colour and device; 16 colours and 24 devices.
Heraldry: Ash can only be used as the border.
Heraldry: the guildmaster chooses on the Guild tab, which shows the banner as you choose.
Heraldry: the first choice is free; each change after costs 500 silver from the silver treasury.
Heraldry: once your guild has heraldry, two banners hang either side of its hall's door.
Rented Rooms: a tenant can now sleep in the home they rent.
Silver: Drakes are now called silver everywhere: account card, Bank, Market and Work tabs, writs, prices and treasury.
dev_note: Nothing else changed. Your balance is exactly what it was, just under the new name.

summary: Silver: Silver ore and the Silver Ingot are still materials as before.
Masonry: work stone at a General Store's bench (50 gold a work) or a home mason's bench (50,000 gold).
Masonry: 2 Rough Stone make 1 Cut Stone, from rank 0.
Masonry: 1 Sulphur, 1 Lead and 5 Rough Stone make 10 Mortar, from rank 10.
Masonry: the chisel scores five lines on the stone; strike the marked line before it moves.
Masonry: each unit gives XP at your rank's own tier, plus 500 the first time you make it.
Mortar: a new Stores material, withdrawn as an item or sold on the market.
Quarryman: rank 50, Rough Stone cuts 1:1, not 2:1.
Builder: rank 50, a seat's fortification projects you begin need 10% less stone.
Fortifier: rank 100, on a seat's defending side you keep its Walls from dropping, once a Season.
Sculptor: rank 100, carve stone furniture: column, bench, font and statue plinth, from Cut Stone and Mortar.
Professions: the Professions page lists Masonry as practised, and the Stores page has the Mason's Bench.
Masonry: a stone work's XP is now said as Masonry's, not Smithing's.
Game: unspecified fixes and improvements.
Game: unspecified fixes and improvements.
Crown Sieges: at Daggerfall, Wayrest and Sentinel the Throne, Gatehouse and camps now stand at the castle's entrance.
Royal Tourney: the ring now stands in the castle's square.
Crown Sieges: two more banners hang either side of the castle's entrance, in the holder's colours.
Guild Tags: a player's tag over their head sits in a frame edged in their guild's colour, with its shield.
Siege Bar: the siege HUD shows the defenders' shield at the left and the challengers' at the right.
Chronicle: each line sits under its guild's shield, and the Hall of Records ends with a Roll of Arms.
Moderation: /siege void lets a Moderator void a seat's battle of the week won by an exploit.
Moderation: before a result, a voided battle is called off and every Sellsword's fee goes home.
Moderation: after a capture, a void returns the Charter to the previous holder with its prior Standing, Tithe and Legacy.
Moderation: after a hold, a void takes away the Standing and next-defence bonus the battle gave.
Moderation: rewards already claimed stay claimed, but no new ones can be claimed from a voided battle.
Standing: a seat's board now says which way the holder's Standing moved since the last Turning.
Festival: while one rules, the town's streets play the tavern's songs, with the holder's banners and lanterns after dusk.
Game: unspecified fixes and improvements.
Glyphs: press a glyph on the account card to hide it, and again to show it.
Glyphs: hiding a glyph only hides the icon; anything the glyph lets you do still works.
Moderation: tabbyvish and Starempire42 are now moderators, with the blue shield and /mute and /unmute.
Online Mode: everyone online is disconnected once when this update goes live, and reconnects.
Enhanced Text: letters are drawn slightly heavier and further apart, so small text no longer blurs.
Enhanced Text: labels, counts, key hints and badges drawn at 9 or 10 pixels are now at least 11.
Enhanced Text: the dim grey used for secondary text is lighter, still quieter than the main text.
Enhanced Font: every Enhanced screen now uses the Enhanced pixel font, with three exceptions.
Enhanced Font: the Features, Overhauls and About pages now use it.
Enhanced Font: character creation's skills and questions now use it.
Enhanced Font: the detail lines on an inventory item's card now use it.
Enhanced Font: the controller bindings headings and the controller prompt bar now use it.
Enhanced Font: the death screen now uses it.
Enhanced Font: the burning-ground warning at Dagon's Breach now uses it.
Enhanced Font: the opening film's credits and buttons now use it.
Enhanced Font: the asset pickers for music, sounds, lighting and Morrowind bodies now use it.
Enhanced Font: the prison countdown and Come Sail Away map help lines now use it, not the 1996 font.
Enhanced Font: in dungeons a readied spell was named twice; only the HUD names it now.
Enhanced Font: the account recovery code keeps its own font so B/8, G/6, S/5 stay distinct.
Enhanced Font: the pages of books stay in the readable book serif.
Enhanced Font: the place names lettered on the map stay in their own font.
Enhanced Font: long labels squeezed into small boxes were fitted so the bigger text still fits.
Timers: a new Timers window online; an hourglass by your profile icon shows shared events with live countdowns.
Timers: it shows Dagon's Breach: when the next opens, and while one stands, when it seals and collapses.
Timers: it shows town raids in your region, the next raid elsewhere and how many are coming today.
Timers: it shows the Sunday Turning at 18:00 UTC and the Friday 18:00 UTC Reckoning when pledges lock.
Timers: it shows this week's sieges, tourneys and revolts, with who fights whom, and any Royal Tourney.
Timers: it shows the Season's end when one is under way.
Timers: it shows when new bounty hunts and raids roll, and the daily reset at 00:00 UTC.
Timers: events running now are listed first with the time until they end; the rest follow, soonest first.
Timers: times are shown in your own clock and the countdowns tick live while the window is open.
Timers: tap outside the window or press Escape (or B on a controller) to close it.
Moderation: voiding a revolt before it is fought no longer saves the Charter; it lapses as at the Turning.
Moderation: a voided capture gives back the holder's building projects, with materials taken back from the stockpile.
Moderation: a guild that gave up its seat before the siege no longer gets it back from a void.
Moderation: voiding a held siege fought before this update leaves the holder's Standing alone.
Moderation: a void can no longer land after the Turning; /siege void says the week is settled.
Ships at Sea: friendly ships have green health bars and a "Friendly" card; fire on her and she turns hostile.
Ships at Sea: every ship is named for her trade and waters; crown ships for their kings, gods and towns.
Ship Tags: within 400 m a ship's tag shows her class and where she's going, such as moored or patrolling.
Ships at Sea: ships fade in and out over a few seconds instead of popping, shadow and flag included.
Online Sea: a ship never blinks; when the sailing player leaves, another nearby takes her over where she lies.
Ships at Sea: packets sail lanes between neighbouring port towns, berth, wait and sail on, on one shared schedule.
Ships at Sea: packets follow the water round headlands, take a free berth, or lie off the port.
Ships at Sea: a packet that is sunk or taken is gone for everyone until her next voyage.
Ships at Sea: the Ships at sea setting decides how many are out near you, none when it's off.
Ship Handling: ships no longer stick on World of Daggerfall's ocean rocks; you can always sail away from a rock.
Ship Handling: ships no longer get stuck in place at sea, and the sails work there again.
Ship Handling: a ship run aground can float off again, and backing off a shore works.
Crew: your crew no longer talks over each other; lines show under the speaker's name, stacked neatly.
Basket: the mouse cursor now appears for the Basket's search so you can click the glints.
Basket: when the search ends, however it ends, the mouse goes back to looking around.
Basket: clicking anywhere while a glint shows still counts, so attack key, trigger and tap work as before.
Basket: with Gentle acts on, the search has nothing to press, so the cursor isn't freed.
Basket: letting go of the click that found the last glint no longer starts picking the same patch's herbs.
Gathering: Mining, Skinning and Fishing take the look back; you aim them with the crosshair.
Revenants: Elite and Champion foes (level 3+) that kill you become your revenant, with a name and epithet.
Revenants: below 20% health a special foe has a 5% chance to flee and become a revenant.
Revenants: one to three in-game days later a revenant can turn up in place of a wilderness encounter, strongest first.
Revenants: each time one kills you or escapes it ranks up, to rank 5, and earns a new epithet.
Revenants: each rank adds +25% health and +10% damage; human foes also gain levels.
Revenants: a foe whose spell, lingering effect or poisoned blade finishes you becomes your revenant too.
Revenants: they are tied to your character and survive reloads; up to 5 can hunt you at once.
Revenants: they follow the Loot rarity setting; turn it off and no new ones are made.
Revenants: every revenant has a personality: Brutal, Witty, Humorous, Arrogant, Cold, Zealous, Unhinged, Honourable, Craven or Weary.
Revenants: a revenant keeps its personality for good; orcs tend brutal, liches cold, daedra arrogant.
Revenants: every moment has its own lines in each voice, from the taunt on return to last words.
Revenants: beasts don't talk; their temperament shows in what they do instead.
Revenants: the card and the Revenants page show each revenant's personality.
Revenants: a beaten revenant yields instead of dying, kneeling to wait for your judgement; nothing can hurt it.
Revenants: walk up to it and use it to choose its fate in the loot window: Kill or Spare.
Revenants: Kill shows the exact weapon it will drop.
Revenants: Spare says where it will go: to your side, or away if companion slots are full.
Revenants: click a choice and confirm, or press K or S then K/S again or Enter; Esc backs out.
Revenants: if left kneeling 90 seconds or you walk away, it escapes, ranks up and remembers.
Revenants: a flying revenant kneels on the ground so you can always reach it.
Revenants: Kill plays an execution: last words, a blow, a blood burst, then the body burns away.
Revenants: an execution counts as your kill: Renown, and a soul for Soul Trap or Azura's Star.
Revenants: an executed revenant drops a unique weapon of its own, plus everything it carried.
Revenants: the weapon fits it: an orc's axe, a lich's staff, a vampire's saber, a barbarian's claymore.
Revenants: the dropped weapon is named for it, such as Grushnak's Reaver or Varis' Requiem.
Revenants: the dropped weapon is Magic, Rare or Legendary, never Common; higher rank gives better odds.
Revenants: an executed revenant is gone for good and listed among the Fallen as Executed.
Revenants: Spare frees it and swears it to you as a companion; it never hunts you again.
Companions: sworn revenants use the crew's companion system, following through doors and fighting at your side.
Companions: they fight with the strength of their rank and go by their own names.
Companions: use one to open its pack and store items.
Companions: each has a card on the party panel and a green health bar overhead.
Companions: slots are limited to 3 at your side, shared between sworn revenants and any ship's crew ashore.
Companions: if your slots are full when you spare one, it waits away until you call it.
Companions: a companion that falls is carried off through a portal to recover for 8 hours.
Companions Page: a new page on the pause menu's Stats rail with a slot strip showing your 3 slots.
Companions Page: At your side shows each companion's portrait, rank, personality and health, with Send away.
Companions Page: Away lists companions waiting or recovering, with Call; it says why one can't come yet.
Companions Page: Release frees a companion for good and hands back its pack, after confirming.
Companions: they talk in their own voice on arrival, sending away, falling, and sometimes in a fight.
Companions: they step through a swirling violet portal when arriving, called, sent away or carried off.
Companions: when they catch up after falling behind they use a pair of portals.
Companions: the figure gathers out of the light on arrival and burns into it on leaving; ship crews ashore too.
Revenants: online, other players see your beaten revenant kneel, burn away when executed, or step into its portal.
Revenants: other players see your revenant by its name.
Revenants: nothing can hit a kneeling revenant, no weapon, arrow or spell.
Revenants: a revenant you've judged can't come back if its poison killed you afterwards.
Revenants: saving while one stands no longer leaves a nameless copy of it behind.
Revenants: one that escaped, was executed or spared no longer leaves a lootable corpse after a dungeon load.
Companions: companion packs follow your save; loading no longer duplicates or loses their items.
Revenants: a spared revenant no longer appears twice for a moment while it steps into its portal.
Companions: spells a companion carried no longer come back after recovering, sending away or loading.
Revenants: the Execute button and confirmed Release are edged in red; the kill choice shows the weapon's card on hover.
Rendering: fixed every sprite vanishing after an execution in a dungeon; elite glow no longer hangs while it burns away.
Revenants: a revenant that only ran no longer boasts of killing you; undead and atronachs aren't Witty.
Elites: in the open world 5%→2% of foes are elite, one at a time, none for about 15 minutes after.
Elites: they no longer appear below foe level 3, and never as city watch or allies.
Elites: elites are named everywhere: on hover, in death notices and on corpses.
Revenants: the cards, kill-or-spare window and Companions page are Enhanced UI; Classic shows text and a keyed box.
Revenants: the revenant card is a HUD piece you can move by unlocking the UI with Alt+U.
Paperdoll: in Firefox the paperdoll is no longer mirrored over the stats under the pack's blurred backdrop.
Online Quests: no quest fails because time ran out online; deadlines and return-before limits never expire.
Online Quests: a step that would make you wait days now moves on after about two minutes of play.
Online Quests: a quest that wraps up a while after you finish now closes within a couple of minutes.
Online Quests: quest text no longer counts days; "you have 7 days" reads "you have a few days".
Online Quests: no countdowns online; the journal, tracker, rail and map markers no longer show "Time remains".
Online Quests: quest letters reach you any time of day, though still only in a town.
Bounties: online, a bounty you take stays yours until you finish or drop it.
Online Quests: vampire and werewolf quests come after a few minutes of play instead of 38 or 84 game days.
Online Quests: Thieves Guild and Dark Brotherhood invitations arrive minutes after you earn them, not three days.
Online Quests: a few quests still follow day and night online; the online day cycle lasts about an hour.
Gear Wear: weapons and armour last twice as long; wear per hit is back to Daggerfall's own rate.
Gear Wear: a dagger or short bow lasts about 25→50 hits.
Guild Hall: Officers and the guildmaster can paint the hall's walls, windows, roof and door from the Exterior tab.
Guild Hall: stand on the hall's lot and press Decorate to furnish its yard, up to sixty pieces.
Guild Hall: taking down or shrinking a yard piece returns half its cost to the guild treasury.
Guild Hall: ranks below Officer and outsiders see the hall's colours and yard but cannot change them.
Game: unspecified fixes and improvements.
Door Griefing: foes no longer stand in doorways, so a crowd can't seal a building or dungeon door.
Door Griefing: clicking a door works with a peaceful guard in front of it; hostile foes still take the click.
Door Griefing: the indoor watch spawns inside the threshold, spread out, instead of stacked on the door.
Foes: guards, bandits, dungeon foes and wilderness encounters push apart across groups so mixed crowds don't overlap.
Cover: trees, crates, barrels, statues and solid decor block sight with Enhanced AI.
Cover: they also stop missiles both ways; area spells still burst where they land.
Cover: grass, flowers, small clutter and see-through props aren't cover; felled trees stop being cover.
Tactics: at most two melee and two ranged foes attack you at once; the rest ring you and wait.
Tactics: melee foes step in when you're open and back out after their blow; a patience clock limits waits.
Tactics: a hurt foe gives ground and circles before coming back.
Tactics: animals and cowardly people flee at low health; guards, undead, daedra and constructs never do.
Tactics: archers and casters back away from a closing melee fighter, fight when cornered, and seek a clear shot.
Tactics: Enhanced AI applies everywhere; with it off, foes behave as in classic Daggerfall.
Telegraphed Attacks: foes of level 10 and up, or elite, have a special wind-up attack, smaller than the world boss's.
Telegraphed Attacks: Lunge is a long lane ahead (beasts, swordsmen).
Telegraphed Attacks: Sweep is a wide cone in front (brutes, blades).
Telegraphed Attacks: Slam is a disc just ahead (giants, atronachs, daedra lords).
Telegraphed Attacks: the shape glows for 0.7 to 0.9 s; step out of it and it misses.
Telegraphed Attacks: a hit does 1.25x to 1.75x a normal blow.
Telegraphed Attacks: each foe has an 8 to 15 second cooldown; only one nearby winds up at once.
Telegraphed Attacks: the ground marks follow slopes and fade into fog.
Dagon's Breach: the Sigil Broker is held in a cage by Dagon's Faithful from the 17:00 omen.
Dagon's Breach: kill every one of the faithful, Summoner included, before the 20:00 breach to free her for everyone.
Dagon's Breach: if someone else already killed the Summoner, killing the rest still frees her.
Dagon's Breach: you can talk to her from any side of the cage.
Dagon's Breach: if the faithful still stand when the breach opens, they pass into it and she stays caged.
Dagon's Breach: once freed, she trades until midnight even if the Warden falls early.
Online Mode: everyone online is disconnected once when this update goes live, and reconnects.
Ship Tags: no tag is drawn over another; the looked-at, then hostile, then nearest ships come first.
Ships at Sea: other players' AI ships now sail smoothly instead of jumping forward or sliding backwards online.
Ship Tags: only one ship shows its second line, the one whose card is up or nearest your crosshair.
Travel Options: changing the settings now takes effect straight away with no relog.
Travel Options: new dial Player Controlled Inns Travel, on by default, makes any trip stopping at inns a journey.
HUD: the lost part of the fatigue, health and magicka bars is now a dim strip, not a pale one.
HUD: the lost-part strip no longer gets stuck; it stays at most about a second before catching up.
Loading: pressing a key while the world loads no longer shows a red crash message.
Swimming: sinking into water no longer puts your view under the ground.
Graphics: likely fix for dark boxes around sprites on Macs with Apple chips.
Enhanced AI: walk up to a foe waiting its turn and it now turns and fights instead of backing away.
Enhanced AI: the step back after a blow is under half a second, then the foe holds its ground.
Enhanced AI: retreating foes walk away facing the way they're going, then turn back to fight.
Enhanced AI: hurt foes back off at most once every 10 seconds.
Enhanced AI: an archer waiting for its turn stands still and faces you, with no strafing.
Enhanced AI: an archer you close in on retreats once, up to 2 seconds, then fights hand to hand.
Enhanced AI: once you're more than about 6 m away, the archer goes back to shooting.
Champions: foes of level 3 or more standing as champions 5%→7%.
Crosshair: hostile champions, elites and revenants are no longer named at the crosshair; the name shows on the health bar.
Crosshair: a non-fighting special foe is still named at the crosshair, such as a sworn companion or a beaten revenant.
Elites: they are back to their old numbers; the last change made them rarer, now undone.
Elites: in the open world 2%→5% of foes stand as elites, with no limit of one at a time.
Elites: ordinary dungeons hold an elite 10%→20% of the time again; Elite Dungeons keep their 3 to 4.
Champions: unchanged; about one foe in twenty of level 3 or more.
Alchemy Station: brew Daggerfall's twenty potions at any Alchemist's (50 gold a brew) or a home station.
Alchemy: ingredients come from your Stores: herbs, vein metals and gems, the sea's Pearl and a body's parts.
Alchemy: cheapest potions from rank 0, resistances and Restore Power from 10, Invisibility at 70, Purification at 90.
Alchemy: one potion a brew, two from Journeyman, three as a Master; Apothecary-goods-only potions brew one at any rank.
Alchemy: a brew may come out Potent; healing, stamina, strength or power potions get +25% magnitude.
Alchemy: XP comes with every brew by the potion's rank, plus 500 the first time you brew each one.
Alchemy: Daggerfall's potion maker with ingredients in your pack is unchanged and earns nothing toward Alchemy.
Brewer: rank 50, three potions a brew at Journeyman.
Distiller: rank 50, +10% Potent chance.
Master Alchemist: rank 100, Potent potions are +40%, not +25%.
Transmuter: rank 100, two of a metal and a Mercury make one of the next up, Tin to Platinum.
Enchanting: the item maker costs 10% less from Journeyman and 20% less as a Master.

Auras: the Seraph Wings are the developers' own aura, worn from the account card's aura picker.
Auras: wings of flowing golden light grow from the wearer's back, with long plumes and short inner feathers.
Auras: the wings breathe slowly and beat once every eight seconds; sparks streak past their tips.
Auras: the wings cast a pool of gold at the wearer's feet and a gold light on the world around.
Auras: the wings sit on the wearer's back on both Morrowind bodies and Eye of the Beholder sprites.
Auras: an aura you put on or take off now shows to everyone around within a second or two.
Auras: up to 32 auras are drawn at once, up from 16.
Auras: a player who drops out of sight for a moment no longer has their aura start over from nothing.
Auras: the cloak and wings now sit at the Eye of the Beholder sprite's real shoulders.
Auras: they face the way your sprite faces; walking backward, the cloak no longer covers your sprite's face.
Auras: the cloak is no longer drawn around your camera in first person.
Auras: while you swim, the cloak folds away and the wings close.
Auras: players in beast form now carry the wings at the beast's own shoulders.
Auras: Golden Radiance no longer vanishes when you look down on its wearer from high above.
Auras: the Seraph Wings' light stays gold in dungeons.
Auras: in first person, looking down no longer washes your view in gold from the wings' backlight.
Auras: after swimming, the Seraph Wings open again when you ride or crouch, and the Holo Shadow Cloak unfolds.
Auras: the tip of every wing strand no longer shows a faint twist.
Auras: on Eye of the Beholder skins the wings now sit farther back and no longer clip through the body.
Auras: before your first step, the wings now hang behind you instead of over your sprite's face.
Auras: the Seraph Wings are slimmer, shorter and softer, with a fainter glow and a dimmer light on the ground.
Arena Bouts: arena fighters now telegraph their heavy blows at each other, not just at you.
Arena Ladder: losing a ladder bout resets that tier's run, and every tier's champion is an elite.
Arena Ladder: no potions or cheese spells (Invisibility, Chameleon, Shadow, Levitate, Calm, Charm, Teleport) in ladder bouts.
Arena Ladder: winning a ladder bout you have won before pays no purse, points or Renown.
Arena Ladder: the online ladder needs a registered account, and each ticket is good for one bout.
Arena Ladder: online, the champions run and look elite, and a time-out needs real damage; a tie is a draw.
Arena Ladder: fixes for a stuck run, champions fleeing as revenants, a worn ring losing its effect, and Recall.
Quests: a quest's foe that is not yet hostile now shows "Quest: <title>" under its name on the enhanced plaque.
Homes: graveyard crypts are no longer sold as homes online; they have no inside.
Quests: The Possessed Child can be finished in Tigonus; a quest person placed in a covered cellar now stands upstairs.
Beautiful Villages: houses and the stone gazebo no longer float; hills are drawn at their real size and shape.
Dying: after you respawn online, paralysis, silence and fatigue or magicka drain are gone; diseases still carry over.
Fishing: Open Water only appears over water, and a net you are winding up can't be thrown onto the sand.
Resting: online, you can rest at a dungeon bed on your floor, as at a campfire.
Loading Screens: starting a game, going online, a door, fast travel, Recall and respawn now show a loading screen.
Loading Screens: the screen shows one of your screenshots with where and when taken, or the night sky.
Loading Screens: it never covers character creation, the pause menu, a level-up or the dream videos.
Loading Screens: choose Your screenshots, Night sky or Off on the new tile under Features (Interface); Classic is unchanged.
Screenshots: the screenshot key (F8) now keeps every shot in a browser gallery, up to 120, never uploaded.
Screenshots: a new Screenshots page on the main menu and the pause menu's System tab opens, saves and deletes shots.
Screenshots: a switch on that page decides whether the key still downloads a PNG as well.
Telegraphed Attacks: hits landed during a wind-up fill a poise meter under its health bar; enough interrupts the attack.
Telegraphed Attacks: iron attacks (red and hatched) cannot be interrupted, such as a giant's slam and an elite's heaviest.
Telegraphed Attacks: an attack that hits nobody leaves its enemy open for about a second, taking 30% more.
Telegraphed Attacks: stepping out in its last moment is a perfect dodge with a longer opening.
Telegraphed Attacks: the body glints as the wind-up begins and again just before it lands, with a sound for each.
Telegraphed Attacks: wind-ups vary in length, lunges track you, blade-fighters sometimes feint and brutes chain two blows.
Telegraphed Attacks: new attacks: the ring, the charge from range, the leap and an archer's aimed shot.
Telegraphed Attacks: champions and revenants telegraph at any level; elites and revenants more often, with their kind's whole set.
Telegraphed Attacks: online, everyone sees an enemy's wind-up and enemies wind up at other players too.
Revenants: a revenant learns from how you beat it and comes back adapted, at most three adaptations, never immunity.
Revenants: each has a hidden weakness; strike it to reveal it; it takes 50% more and staggers twice as easily.
Revenants: from rank 3 its will must be broken before it kneels, or it escapes the killing blow, stronger.
Revenants: from rank 3 the first killing blow brings it back at 30%, 35% or 40% health by rank, once.
Revenants: from rank 2 it has a named signature attack, iron from rank 3, and one to three kin.
Revenants: each has a lair, a named dungeon near where it was made; townsfolk may tell you where.
Revenants: online, one that kills you takes an unlocked item; kill or spare it to get it back.
Revenants: left alone past its due day it festers and grows stronger, ranking up on its own three times over.
Revenants: a special enemy that knocks out your companion, or one you run from, becomes a revenant too.
Companions: sworn companions have loyalty; neglected they desert, and a disloyal Unhinged, Craven or Brutal one may turn on you.
Revenants: the Revenants page and card show everything you know: habits, weakness, will, signature, band, lair and what it took.
Living World: every town's people are residents with a name, face, home and trade, kept for good.
Living World: each resident has a day: rise, work, errands, friends, evening and home; the watch keeps shifts.
Living World: online, everyone sees the same people in the same places at the same time.
Living World: townsfolk stop and talk among themselves, and greet you by name once they count you a friend.
Living World: step into a tavern, shop, temple or house and the people whose day has them there are inside.
Living World: merchants, pilgrims, couriers, pedlars and adventurers travel between towns by day and camp by night.
Living World: travellers meet the land's monsters; you can fight beside a party under attack and they remember it.
Living World: in port towns, sailors crew the ships that call there, and travellers sail across the Bay.
Living World: on the Overworld, parties on the road are marked, and a party in trouble shows in red.
Living World: adventurers dive the dungeons near their towns; meet a company down there and they fight at your side.
Living World: some adventurers never come up; their remains lie three days with a keepsake for their family.
Living World: what you do changes how people feel about you: kindness, help, theft or crime.
Living World: a friend greets you by name and aids you on the road; an enemy won't speak.
Living World: striking down a resident is permanent; their household turns against you and every witness counts the crime.
Chronicle: the chronicle (L) has a new People page: your friends, enemies, the people who know you, and the dead.
Travel Options: the speed dials are gone; journeys run x100 on a road or track and x60 off it.
Travel: wilderness enemies only come for a fast traveller who fails a Stealth check; a noticing enemy wears a !.
Travel: online, the ship's time dial is gone; time at sea keeps the world's pace.
Living World: on by default under Features (World); off, or on Classic UI, towns keep Daggerfall's townsfolk.
Living World: its work in the largest city was cut from up to 120 ms a frame to a few.
Vanilla Enhanced: carademono's remaster of Daggerfall's own textures now ships with the game and is the default look.
Texture Overhaul: pick Classic on the card for Daggerfall's own textures; it switches your texture mods off without removing them.
Texture Overhaul: with Vanilla Enhanced on, the card offers Masked Roads and Snowless Swamps and Jungles as switches.
Texture Overhaul: the new textures are decoded in the background, so loading them doesn't stutter the game.
Texture Mods: they load in Daggerfall Unity's order; where two carry a texture, the later one is drawn.
Texture Mods: each can be switched off and on without removing it, on the Replacement packs card.
Texture Mods: switching texture mods mid-game now applies to everything drawn after the switch, not a mix until reload.
Texture Overhaul: the main menu card now sees attached texture mods; it could show Classic with mods on.
Texture Mods: an unreadable mod is listed on the Replacement packs card with the reason and a Remove button.
Texture Overhaul: with a loose pack attached, the card explains why Classic can't be picked.
Vanilla Enhanced: your own attached copy, such as a newer Nexus Mods one, is used instead of the built-in.
Texture Mods: ground textures now appear on terrain, as in Daggerfall Unity, from a loose pack or tile mod.
Main Menu: two new icons in the top-left corner, Patreon and Ko-fi, each opening its page in your browser.
Main Menu: it is no longer cut off on short windows; the logo shows in full and the menu scrolls.
Main Menu: on narrow and mid-size windows the logo now sits below the corner icons and your profile picture.
Website: it now offers Ko-fi beside Patreon in its top-right corner.
Spell Bursts: Fire lands as a fireball bloom with embers, licking flame, a scorch glow and a shock ring.
Spell Bursts: Frost lands as a splash crown of droplets, ice glints on the floor and cold mist.
Spell Bursts: Shock lands as jagged lightning arcs from the impact into the floor, with fast sparks.
Spell Bursts: Poison lands as green globs that splat into bubbling pools under a sickly vapour.
Spell Bursts: Magic lands as motes spiralling out over rune rings.
Spell Bursts: Heal lands as a soft green floor glow with thin lines of light rising, no shockwave.
Spell Bursts: each burst takes its colour from that element's own spell art; touch spells now show a small burst.
Area Spells: Area at Range and Around Caster show what they catch: people to 4.45 m, the boss 5.8 m.
Area Spells: the shockwave spreads across what the spell hit; a fireball on a wall bursts as a ring there.
Area Spells: bigger areas show more; the element breaks out across the whole area, and area heals fill the circle.
Spell Bursts: impacts briefly light up the walls and floor around them in the element's colour.
Spell Sounds: Fire is a whumpf and crackle; Frost a splash with ice tinkles; Shock a lightning crack and buzz.
Spell Sounds: Poison is a squelch and bubbles; Magic a resonant thoom; Heal a new healing shimmer.
Spell Bursts: the classic flash, the bloom and the camera kick stay; there are fewer element-art sparks now.
Spell Bursts: sparks no longer jump away when the world recentres mid-burst or linger after a load.
Interface: text and buttons no longer show a blue selection highlight on click or drag; fields can be selected.
Decorator: it offers the town mods' furnishings while they're on, adding 297 pieces such as beds and rugs.
Decorator: turning a town mod on or off changes what the decorator offers within a second.
Decorator: it now offers what Daggerfall stands in its dungeons: thrones, cages, coffins, statues, chains, braziers and more.
Decorator: a yard now offers Daggerfall's street pieces and the trees and plants of its own town's climate.
Decorator: a tree or plant placed in a yard shows its own picture under In this yard.
Low Poly Trees: a yard tree is the 3D tree up close and its picture far away, sized as placed.
Low Poly Trees: a yard tree whose picture was loading as you travelled no longer appears far from its yard.
Hired Traders: with Show Nudity off, the Vendors category no longer offers nude figures; placed ones show their clothed stand-in.
Arena Crowd: the Arena crowd no longer seats nude figures while Show Nudity is off.
Titles: Flylighter now holds the Crystal Fist title, shown in purple, with a glyph of three purple slashes.
Titles: Flylighter keeps the Disciple title too; pick which to wear from the account card.
Auras: Crystal Resonance is a ring of tiny purple squares about the feet, stacked into columns that rise and fall.
Auras: it comes with the Crystal Fist title; wear it from the account card's Aura row.
Auras: on an Eye of the Beholder character, the developers' wings stay lined up with the sprite as it turns.
Auras: this holds on a key press, while the camera moves round, in the saddle, and on other players.
Developers: RookieG is now a developer.
Dungeon Map: steep ramps in hallways now fill in on the 3D dungeon map once you have walked them.
Boats: a boat whose hold is too heavy to carry packed can no longer be picked up into unmoveable parts.
Teleporters: red brick teleporters you walk into now always send you on; before, some only worked when clicked.
Companions: sworn revenants and crew ashore now attack the enemy fighting you, not an idle one behind a wall.
Quests: if you saved in The Haunted House with the foe sealed in, it now stands by the hatch.
Loot Drops: regular enemies keep 3 in 4 items offline, up from half; online 5/8 to 7/8 by Renown.
Loot Drops: regular enemies drop blue, yellow and orange items more often, and online the boost grows with your Renown.
Loot Drops: the boost steps up at Renown 10, 20, 30 and 40, the same steps sigils use.
Loot Drops: the Renown that counts is the rolling player's; the host's in a shared dungeon.
Loot Drops: gear an enemy was wearing can now drop as Magic, Rare or better, champions, elites and bosses included.
Loot Drops: after you loaded a save, the worn gear of enemies already in the world dropped plain again.
Loot Drops: when a body is full, it keeps a potion or rest supply ahead of plain gear.
Healing Potions: about 1 enemy in 33→13 carries one, and about 1 dungeon treasure pile in 5.
Restore Power Potions: they now drop too: about 1 enemy in 20, and 1 treasure pile in 10.
Rest Supplies: they now drop online and more often: about 1 enemy in 14 carries one.
Loot Drops: these are offline chances and online chances at Renown 20; at Renown 1 the boost is half.
Ember Jar: other players saw your Ember Jar's fire as a plain campfire.
Silver Finds: about one harvest in ten finds 2-5 silver, up to 30 silver a day.
Silver Finds: bodies, piles and searches hold 1-4 silver, about 1 in 20, 8 and 7.
Silver Finds: each body or pile gets one chance, so leaving a dungeon and coming back doesn't roll it again.
Silver Finds: if a find can't reach your account, it is kept and sent later, even after a reload.
Silver Finds: found silver shows as a card or in chat; the Bank panel shows the day's total.
Silver Finds: they need you online and signed in with a registered account at least a week old.
Sea Serpent: every hoard now holds a Deadlands Ember, spent at the Sigil Broker's insignia counter.
Coilscale: a ship that fought the serpent has a 1 in 4 chance to find a piece of Sethrakul's Coilscale.
Coilscale: Sea-Scale (2 pieces) gives frost resistance and Endurance.
Coilscale: Constrict (4 pieces) makes each weapon hit make your next hits on that enemy stronger, stacking to 5.
Coilscale: Shed Skin (6 pieces) heals you when a hit takes you below 35% health, then recovers for minutes.
Sea Serpent: slaying it now pays 40 silver (20 for a ship standing by), toward the same 150 a day.
Arena Bouts: set bonuses, sigil weapon bonuses and Legendary powers now switch off in bouts against other players.
Wallet: every character now carries a Wallet; new characters start with one and existing ones receive it on next load.
Wallet: it holds your letters of credit, Deadlands Embers and Welkynd Shards, and shows your gold and, online, silver.
Wallet: in the Enhanced inventory, letters of credit, Embers and Shards move off the pages into the Wallet on Valuables.
Wallet: in the classic inventory nothing moves; the Wallet is on the Clothing & Misc page.
Wallet: on the hotbar, pressing the Wallet shows what it holds and fetches your silver for the next press.
Wallet: it weighs nothing and never leaves your pack; it can't be dropped, sold, traded or stolen by revenants.
Wallet: letters of credit now show on the Valuables page in the Enhanced inventory; they were filed under Misc.
City Watch: fixed a crash when a watchman died from his own attack, such as a Ring of Namira reflection.
City Watch: a watchman no longer flickers out of sight each time he lands a blow on a monster.
Town Watch: the watch keeps the town day and night in three eight-hour shifts plus a day off.
Town Watch: patrols walk in pairs around their own district; in larger towns a watchman stands at each gate.
Town Watch: off duty, a watchman wears his own clothes as a townsperson; larger towns keep a larger watch.
Town Watch: a watchman on duty greets you by your standing with the region's law.
Town Watch: a first minor offence in a region draws a Hold! warning, not an arrest; the next brings one.
Town Watch: a monster that gets into town can now attack townspeople; one blow kills a townsperson.
Town Watch: the watch now defends townspeople a monster is attacking, as it does when a monster attacks you.
Townspeople: they run from a monster that comes close, along the street rather than through walls, and keep their distance.
Town Watch: the watch no longer shouts "Halt!" over and over; one watchman calls, at most once every 15 seconds.
Town Watch: all of this is in the living world; Classic play keeps Daggerfall's own watch and townspeople.
Townspeople: those who stop to talk now turn to face each other instead of all facing you.
Townspeople: a group waits until all have walked over, then takes turns; you hear them only then.
Townspeople: people keep the same company about two minutes before moving on, up from 40 seconds.
Townspeople: much less repetition; trades, mornings, days, evenings and nights have more to say, and no conversation repeats twice running.
Townspeople: indoors, people at a table start talking as soon as they sit down together.
Townspeople: a stranger who said nothing as you passed now speaks when you stop in front of them.
Town Watch: paying your fine no longer counts as killing the watchman who walked away.
Town Watch: a townsperson turned guard keeps who they are; a watchman killed by a monster is mourned.
Town Watch: two simultaneous crimes no longer bring more guards than the limit or make one guard twice.
Town Watch: online, another player's watch no longer shows the same watchman twice.
Town Watch: in the biggest cities the watch reaches its post by shift start and stays to the end.
Foe Health Bar: the dark box under a health bar is gone; a resting foe shows only its wind-up track.
Quick Slots: with the diamond style, status-effect icons beside the diamond no longer sit on a dark box.
Quick Slots: an empty spell quick-slot no longer leaves a gap under it that pushed the quick block up.
Ship Plate: at sea, an empty fire-barrel battery no longer stretches the gun rose on the ship plate.
Townspeople: they no longer stand inside building walls or out over the harbour water; where they stop is open street.
Townspeople: they no longer walk on the spot while the game works out their next route, mostly in big cities.
Travellers: on coastal roads they no longer camp, fight or leave their fallen in the sea.
Online Players: other players no longer run in place when their movement stops reaching you; they stand still until they move again, including players who had gone quiet before you arrived.
Crowds: distant players in a big crowd walk smoothly instead of stopping and starting when their computer runs at a low frame rate.
Steady Shadows: lantern shadows cost much less to prepare; each lantern looks once at what can reach it and a still scene does not look at all, with the shadows themselves unchanged.
Chat Window: the player list no longer rebuilds and re-sorts every frame while the chat is open, and the friends list sorts faster.
Performance: settings are read a little faster everywhere.

Quests: quests that would not start in towns redesigned by Beautiful Villages and Beautiful Cities now start, using the nearest town with a missing building such as a second tavern, enough houses, a weaponsmith or a pawnshop; a quest that never fit a town in Daggerfall's own layout still isn't offered there.
Quests: Pothago's Dark Brotherhood contract that needs a weaponsmith now starts, using the nearest one in the next region.
Quests: a quest character whose usual building is gone from their town lives in a house of that town, not in another town.

Quests: Thieves Guild and Dark Brotherhood contracts can be handed in again after a town's layout changes, a temple priest is always found in their own god's temple, and a questor still standing where you met them stays there.
Quests: shared party quests no longer move their quest location to another building every time the party syncs, and party members see the same house name.
Quests: an item or person placed in a quest building after it was shared now appears for every party member.
Temples: every Beautiful Villages temple has its god's Daedra summoner again, standing apart from the priest so clicking the priest always reaches the priest.
Helm Panel: at the helm the ship's speed through the water shows beside her name, in knots.

Ship Handling: no more tacking: the ship sails on every heading, making a little over half her best speed pointed straight into the wind where before she stalled or was blown backwards, and fastest with the wind behind her, off to one side.
Ship Handling: ships are faster under sail, and a galleon with the wind on her side is nearly two thirds faster than before.
Ship Handling: a storm still drives the ship harder, up to twice what a fair breeze does, and in fog she keeps nearly a third of her speed instead of lying becalmed.
Ship Handling: ships still gather speed, lose it and answer the helm as before, but turn on a wider circle at their new, faster speed.
Sails: sails no longer flap uselessly or blow backwards when pointed into the wind, and the ship can no longer get stuck in irons.
Helm Controls: the helm trims the sails itself, so the trim buttons and keys are gone under Responsive handling.
Sailing: Overworld travel by sea sails straight for a port that lies upwind instead of zig-zagging, steers well clear of islands at the new speeds and sails through fog instead of rowing.
Boarding: heaving to beside a ship that has struck her colours stops the player within boarding reach, and at storm speeds it is offered early enough to stop alongside.
Ship Handling: rowing after striking sail no longer holds speed; the ship slows as fast as with no oars out, then rows on.
Online Sea: in a storm a galleon or Carrack no longer vanishes from other players' screens.
Online Sea: a short hiccup in the connection no longer puts the player off a friend's ship they are riding on.

Sea Serpent: it no longer teleports and swims every move it makes, dashing at the player under the water with a wake on the surface showing where it is going, and the Maelstrom now forms where the serpent is swimming, always inside its waters.
Sea Serpent: a Rising Maw, a coil, a spit or a ram is aimed where the player's ship will be when it lands, so turning or slowing when it is seen coming matters.

Sea Serpent: if the player is too far for it to reach in time it surges at them above the water, where their guns can hit it, faster than they are sailing up to its own top speed, and gives up after about 12 seconds of being outsailed.
Sea Serpent: a broadside is judged where the serpent was when the shot landed, so a volley fired just before it moves is no longer wasted.

Sea Serpent: while exactly two ships are fighting it its attacks deal two thirds of their damage, crew losses included; a rowboat or a friend riding on the deck is not a second ship, in fair weather one ship alone still cannot beat it, and three or more ships take full damage.
Sea Serpent: a coil wraps round the ship the way its body lies, and no longer sweeps across the deck as it closes and lets go.
Sea Serpent: a short drop in the connection no longer throws the serpent back across the water on reconnect, and if everyone sails away and comes back later it is where it was, not somewhere new.
Sea Serpent: its wake no longer crowds out the splashes of the player's own cannon fire.
Sea Serpent: an older version of the game is told to reload and cannot fight until it has, and while it reloads it no longer counts as a ship in the fight.
Sea Serpent: it moves smoothly on every screen, even for players whose connection lags behind, and no longer jumps when a relay restarts.
Sea Serpent: a ship that wrecks inside a coil is let go.

Login: logins no longer fail for everyone; yards are only fetched for towns near the player, the server keeps a short copy instead of asking its database each time, and a failed fetch waits longer each time instead of retrying every 10 seconds.
dev_note: The account server was overwhelmed by every game checking every town's yard decorations each minute.

summary: Crew: the crew lasts twice as long: cannon fire, fires on deck, rams and the sea serpent's blows all take half as many men, so against a ship of the line the hull now gives out before the crew does.
Crew: swivel-gun boats (pirate sloops, coasting traders) still go for the player's crew first but at half the old pace, and enemy crews are unchanged.

Small Ship: the player's galleon's broadside hits like six guns: with five gunports a side, one fewer than the old galleon, each ball now does 20% more damage to hulls and sails, and pirates size the galleon up by it; enemy captains' galleons are unchanged.

Cite Tool: no gameplay changes; the developers' notes and code comments that point at specific places in the game's code now name the code itself instead of a line number, so updates no longer collide over them and releases go faster.

Cite Tool: hundreds of those pointers were wrong and are fixed: each was checked against the code it was first written for and the ones that had drifted were moved back, so the game's design notes describe the game accurately again.
Yard: a decoration can stand at most 4 m above the ground, so stacking pieces into towers is no longer possible, and the decorator says why when a piece is placed or moved higher.
Yard: pieces already standing higher than 4 m stay where they are and can still be moved down or removed.

Decorate: in the Decorate panel's In this room and In this yard views, Turn left and Turn right turn a placed piece 15 degrees where it stands, at once and for free, without picking it up; a flat picture flips to face the other way, and doors still turn with their doorway (Move).
Decorate: changing a piece's light, storage or station while it is being turned no longer undoes the other change.

Project Legacy: Project Legacy by Lattymoy, Ghð§† and Positronico is now part of the game and on by default (off on its tile in Features); every new character founds a house with a surname, a seat in the first town they stand in and often a brother or sister, unless the player chooses No lineage online.
Project Legacy: when creating a character the player chooses how death works for their house; online the realm keeps the house and the choice is an Enhanced Plus popup with a third answer.

Project Legacy: Enduring: death is not the end but costs years of life taken by Arkay according to the race's lifespan, in old age the player may pass the mantle to an heir, and when the years run out the line carries on.
Project Legacy: Bloodline: death is final and a Succession window opens to pick who takes the mantle, any living family member or, if the fallen was meant to have an heir, a newborn child of theirs.

Project Legacy: No lineage (online): no house and no heirs, and death works as it always has online; offline the choice keeps its two answers and playing there without a house means turning Project Legacy off in Features.
Project Legacy: heirs are born, not copied, with stats, skills, career and race drawn from their parents' and a share of the family estate of up to 9,900 gold paid as a letter of credit.

Project Legacy: a character with a one-word name founds a house named for its seat, so the first town reached makes the family the house "of Sentinel", brothers and sisters included, and the game says so.
Heirlooms: a fallen character may leave behind an heirloom, their most valuable worn weapon or armour, renamed for the house.

Heirlooms: the remains lie where the character fell together with the heirloom and part of their purse, and the heir gets the death quest The Bones of (name), in the journal, followed by the Quest Guide and circled on the map; reaching the spot opens the remains like a container and what is left stays for the next visit.
Heirlooms: if the bones are sold or dropped they return to where the ancestor fell.

Heirlooms: laying the remains to rest at a temple or at the family seat gives the ancestor's blessing (+3 to their best skill, at most +9 on any one skill), and the heirloom grows stronger with each generation that carries it home.
Family in the World: family members not being played live in the world, in the family home chosen on the Family tab's House page, or with no house in a house the family's seat town lends them.
Family in the World: they keep a daily routine like the town's other residents, asleep at home at night and out in the market and the streets by day.

Family in the World: a family member already played appears in their own body, with their race and the gear they wore at their last save drawn the way other players are drawn online (set by the Other players card in Features), while one never played wears the town's own clothes.

Family in the World: talking to one greets the player as family and offers Play as, a normal Talk or Goodbye, saving the current character first, and a member never played starts out in the town where they were met.

Family in the World: saving a character inside one of the family's houses leaves them waiting there when the player switches to someone else, while saving anywhere else leaves them on their own journey until played again.
Family in the World: in conversation a family member shows their own face, the one picked when they were created.
Family in the World: a family member the player kills is dead for good and the House page records who killed them, and one a monster kills in the street is dead for good too and the town hears of it.
Family in the World: on by default and can be turned off with Family In World in Project Legacy's settings.
Courtship and Marriage: a townsperson who counts the player a friend can be courted by asking about Courtship in conversation, once a day, and how it goes depends on Personality, Etiquette and tone.

Courtship and Marriage: when their heart is full the player can ask for their hand (Marriage) and is wed at the temple of their town, asked whether to marry there and whether they take the house's name.

Courtship and Marriage: the spouse joins the house, keeping their own face and day, and lives in the family's house in their town if the line has one there, otherwise in their own home; every thirty days there is a one-in-four chance of a child, at most six with each spouse, and children cannot be played until the mantle passes to them.
Courtship and Marriage: if someone being courted dies, the courtship ends.

Project Legacy: a child born to the house inherits part of their parent's reputation: a quarter of their standing with each region's law and each guild, and half of how each townsperson felt about them, and a grudge carries over too.
Project Legacy: towns talk about the house: a death, a laying to rest, a wedding and a birth are news for a week in the town where it happened and in the family's seat.
Revenants: the revenant that killed an ancestor comes after their heir, and the journal and the House page name it.

Project Legacy: characters made before this update have no house online, because online a house is founded only when a character is made, so existing characters play as before and their Family tab says why.
Project Legacy: online the family lives in the realm, so every device played on sees the same house, its living and its dead.

Project Legacy: Bloodline is open online: a Bloodline death is final everywhere with no older save on any device able to be played past it, and the heir chosen is born into the realm as that member of the family.

Project Legacy: the house's name shows under the player's name online, over their head, on the Inspect card and on the character list, with a skull marking a Bloodline and the numeral the second of the house to bear that name.

Courtship and Marriage: two players can wed by standing in a temple together, inspecting the other and pressing Propose marriage, which they answer yes or no; each keeps their own house, each family records the other as a spouse, and children come to each house in its own time.
Courtship and Marriage: if a spouse's character dies or is deleted, word reaches the player the next time they are online (within ten minutes if they are), and they may wed again.
Project Legacy: a fallen character's Stores, professions and market place fall with them, so nothing of theirs can be withdrawn or used after their death.
Project Legacy: the homes owned in the realm are the family's houses, where the family lives and a character saved in one waits, just as offline.

Family Tab: the pause window has a new Family tab, between Holdings and System, with the Tree (zoom, pan, play as a sibling, pass the mantle, and where each member lives), the House (model, seat, generations, the living and the fallen, and homes) and the Hall of Ancestors (every house founded); keypad / opens it.

Family Tab: the character sheet (the Stats tab) shows the house, its model and the player's generation, and in an Enduring house the age against the lifespan, the years Arkay has taken, and when the player becomes an elder.

Project Legacy: a permadeath can no longer be undone by quick-loading, closing the game under the death screen or a second tab of the same family; the death is recorded the moment it happens, and if the browser's storage refuses to save it the player is told and it is tried again.

Project Legacy: loading an older save of a fallen or retired family member shows the house's waiting Succession, or offers the member who carries the line now, instead of letting the player play the past.
Project Legacy: an heir is saved the moment they are born, and if that first save fails nothing is lost: reloading births them again, inheritance and all.
Heirlooms: an heirloom can't be taken twice by rewinding or switching between family members, and an ancestor's remains can't be stashed in a chest to make a second set of bones.

Project Legacy: a character copied from online to offline play starts a family of their own instead of sharing the original's (none if it chose No lineage), and one copied into online play has no house there, like any character made before this update.
Project Legacy: holding a key can't confirm a choice by accident: the line's end and Play as at a family meeting both ask twice, and the Family tab can be walked with Tab.

Project Legacy: fixes from the original mod: the heir no longer inherits the dead character's leftover state, sibling kits use the sibling's own race and class, and switching characters no longer drops the player at the map's corner.
Leveling: online characters are no longer forced onto Oblivion leveling: a new online character levels the Daggerfall way and the Oblivion option is shown locked as Offline characters only.
Leveling: characters already using Oblivion leveling online keep it.
Bring Online: an offline Oblivion-leveling character brought online switches to Daggerfall leveling, starting from its current level and keeping any level-up it had already earned.

Leveling: online characters on Oblivion leveling switch to Daggerfall leveling the next time they are played, keeping their level, skills and any level-up already earned, with a message once the world loads.

Character Creation: on the Project Legacy question (Enduring, Bloodline, No lineage) and the leveling question, moving the mouse no longer jumps the highlight between options; the option under the pointer is highlighted and clicking it selects it.

Accounts: the account server no longer falls over again and leaves homes and yards without their decorations; games now wait longer after each failed ask, so a busy minute passes instead of turning into an outage.
dev_note: When the server slowed down, every game asked it again within seconds, and that kept it down.

summary: Login: signing into a room after a slow server answer no longer asks for a second sign-in ticket, so the player reconnects sooner.
Accounts: signing in, joining a room and loading a town's house layouts now cost the account server far less work, so busy evenings are less likely to slow it down or leave decorations missing.
Project Legacy: an online family that has not changed since the last checkpoint is no longer uploaded again at every checkpoint.

Living World: with the living world on, 407 of the game's 410 cities (Ripmarket among them) had nobody walking their streets at any hour because townspeople were laid out on the fields' side of the city walls, where none of their doors are; the streets now fill again by day, travellers leave by the gates and the watch keeps its posts there, and Daggerfall, Wayrest and Sentinel were not affected.

Town Watch: in 14 cities whose palace stands in its own walled grounds (Sentinel among them) the whole city watch lived at the palace and never came out; it now lives where its door opens onto the streets, so it walks its patrols and keeps its posts.
Townspeople: people waiting at the same spot keep a little room from one another and from the groups talking there.
Townspeople: two people who leave a shop or a tavern at the same moment walk out in single file.
Townspeople: a walker steps aside, keeping right, for anyone standing or coming the other way.
Townspeople: in the towns measured, between a tenth and over half of the people in view at midday or in the evening were standing inside someone else, and now almost nobody is.
Townspeople: the town square now has several gathering points across it, and each townsperson keeps to their own.
Townspeople: every neighbourhood has a corner where its people meet, and people's favourite places are the ones near their homes.
Townspeople: stall-keepers set up either at the square or at their own market.
Townspeople: people head out for the evening, and to the morning market, at their own time instead of all on the hour.
Townspeople: in the towns measured, the busiest spot in the evening went from 30 to 64 people, all around one point of the square, to 6 to 17.
Townspeople: a townsperson who stops for the player now stays exactly where they stopped.

Living World: townspeople belong to the guild of their trade or class (scholars, booksellers' and alchemists' people and mages to the Mages Guild, smiths and fighters to the Fighters Guild, courtiers and knights to the town's knightly order) and each spends an evening at their guild hall twice a week.
Living World: sellswords and adventurers now go to their own guild's hall instead of whichever hall is nearest.

Living World: errands go into a shop more often, and to a shop the person has business at: shopkeepers bank their takings, scholars visit the library and the bookseller, and households the general store and the clothier.
Living World: the people found inside a guild hall are now its own guild's members, and Daggerfall's guild halls see 18 visitors a day instead of 12 and its banks 7 instead of 2.
Living World: travellers staying at a tavern, sailors ashore and adventurers who live there each have a room by one of its beds.
Living World: lodgers are up in their room in the morning and again before bed, come down to the common room for breakfast and supper, and sleep out of sight.
Living World: a room the player rents is never given to a lodger.

Townspeople: guild members walk the streets in their guild's classes (Mages Guild members in a mage's hooded robes, Fighters Guild members in a warrior's arms and armour, the knights of an order as knights), priests wear the healer's robes, and adventurers, sellswords and couriers wear their own class all day, not only on their way out of town.

Townspeople: someone keeping their place on their own appears as one of Daggerfall's own pictures of their kind, such as an old beggar at their pitch, a merchant, blacksmith or porter at their stall, a monk at the temple door in the morning or a lord or lady at home in the palace, with several pictures of each kind and the animated ones moving as they do in the game.
Townspeople: they become themselves again the moment they walk on or join a conversation, and a look never changes while the player is watching.
Townspeople: in Daggerfall city, 24 of its 317 people now walk in a class and 17 to 28 stand as still pictures by day.
Waypoints: right-clicking the Overworld or the world map (V) places a waypoint with a name and a flag colour, set for the player alone, their party or their guild.
Waypoints: party and guild waypoints are shared with the other members; only the player who placed one can change it for everyone, while anyone can rename or remove one on their own screen.
Waypoints: a waypoint can be followed from the Overworld's filters, where it stays marked at the edge of the screen with its distance, and its own menu can send the player travelling there.
Waypoints: leaving a party or a guild removes its waypoints.
Travel Options: two speed dials return while travelling, one for the journey's speed and one for the speed while enemies are near, each going x5, x10, x20, x30, x40 and x60 and x100 on a road only.
Travel Options: leaving a road drops a dial at x100 to x60 at once and it does not climb back by itself, and journeys start at x60, so the dial is turned up to x100 on a road.
Travel Options: the dials are in every interface: the Overworld's panel, the Enhanced journey bar, and a small speed box with the classic interface and GrimoireUI.
Overworld: the filters now sit in their own box at the bottom left, which folds away and can be moved like the rest of the HUD.
Foe Health Bar: an enemy's health bar no longer shows an empty box under it; the poise bar appears only when there is something to show, and the bar has one shadow instead of two.

Enhanced Lighting: with Enhanced Lighting on, shadows no longer blink all at once in some rooms; the shadow cache behind it is now off by default and can be turned back on under Enhanced Lighting with Shadow cache (faster, may flicker).
Steady Shadows: shadows hold steady through a brief hitch instead of flashing.
Townspeople: a cat no longer meows many times a second while the player looks at certain townspeople (reported in Chesterwark).

Quests: Protect an Honored Mage (Mages Guild) works online again: the three-hour guard could end before the assassins came, leaving the quest impossible to finish, so the guard now lasts its full three hours of play and the attack always comes inside it, though a guard that already ended this way stays unfinished.

Morrowind Body: steel armour has a new look on the Morrowind body: a full suit of plate - breastplate, pauldrons, gauntlets, greaves, boots and helm - made for the port. Only Steel changes. Silver and Elven armour keep the Morrowind steel they wore before.
Features: a new switch under Features > Combat, Steel Helm: Closed (a visor and a blue plume, the default) or Open (a nasal helm with a mail aventail that shows the face).
Grass: can now be a meadow of new hand-drawn sprites - tall and short green tufts, flowering tufts, dry tufts and bushes - mixed across the land
Grass: every tuft and bush grows to its own size, and whole patches run taller or shorter so the land no longer looks the same everywhere
Grass: flowers gather in lush patches, dry grass in poor ones, and bushes appear here and there from shin-high to shoulder-high
Grass: the meadow does not turn to face you; each tuft and bush stands on crossed cards like the low-poly trees, so it is seen from every side and a low sun lights one face more than the other

Grass: the meadow follows the ground, its greens take the colour of the grass they grow on to fit every climate and season (flowers keep their own colours), and each tuft stands on the slope on a hillside
Grass: the meadow sways in the wind the way the trees do, with bushes stiffer than grass
Grass: the meadow does about the same vertex work as the old pixel tufts
Grass: crossing into a new part of the map no longer makes all the grass, and the trees, jump to a new pose in the wind
Grass: pixel-style tufts no longer swap to different pictures when you cross into a new part of the map
Grass: is now off by default and is turned on under Settings > Grass with Full, Half or Quarter; a Full setting resets to off until turned back on, while Half and Quarter are kept
Grass: the Style setting defaults to Meadow, with Pixel (the old tufts) and Smooth still available
Wind: the Trees sway setting is now just Sway, moving the grass as well as the trees, and turning it off holds both still
Gear Wear: every weapon type now has the same base condition, the Warhammer's 1,600, where daggers, tantos and short bows started at 50 and long bows at 100
Gear Wear: enchanted weapons gain the most: a Cast-When-Strikes enchantment costs 10 condition a strike, so an iron Worm's Tooth lasts 160 strikes instead of 5

Gear Wear: a Cast-When-Held enchantment pays its spell's casting cost in condition the first time it is equipped, no longer breaking an iron dagger, tanto or short bow on the spot; the weapon keeps the rest and lasts about four game days
Gear Wear: bows no longer break after a couple of dozen hits: an iron short bow takes about 800 hits of 20 damage
Gear Wear: light weapons and bows cost less to keep up, because a repair is priced by the share of condition lost

Gear Wear: weapons are updated when a save loads and keep the same percentage of condition, so a broken weapon stays broken and a half-worn dagger is half of its new pool; weapons from the online market, a guild vault or a trade are updated the first time they take wear

Saves: on load, older items get their fixes wherever the save keeps them, not only in the pack, wagon and containers: weapons move to the new condition pool, items made with no condition get one, Roleplay & Realism armour regains the Brigandine, Fur or Mail word, old Sigil Stones are named Deadlands Embers, and a rolled jewel on an unwearable Wand becomes an Amulet
Saves: load fixes now also reach things set out in the house, quest items, a revenant's takings and a sworn revenant's pack, enemies' and guards' gear, and Project Legacy's bequests and remains
Project Legacy: an heir's bequest gets the same load fixes when it is paid, and a fallen relative's remains get them when opened
Saves: a rolled Wand set out in the house becomes an Amulet but still looks like a wand where it stands until picked up
Customs: counts gold and letters of credit in a sworn revenant companion's pack, the same as a crew companion's pack; before, a revenant could carry any amount across uncapped

Homes: a home the Arena moved no longer has its storage emptied at login (chests, storage pieces and things in the room); the move no longer touches a home its owner already lives in, and items already lost are not restored
Beautiful Cities: the crate of belongings that comes with a moved house now shows up in the new house when the city uses the Beautiful Cities layout

Notice Board: each town has one Notice Board, the board nearest the town's middle, in towns with three or more bulletin boards; the other boards are Daggerfall's rumour boards again, as offline, and Bounty Boards are unchanged
Notice Board: says "Notice Board" when you point at it
Notice Board: notes stand straight, the text is larger, and anything written on the cork sits on a dark panel
Notice Board: on a phone the tab row scrolls sideways so Guilds and Seat can be reached
Notice Board: tabs show counts: new notes on Notices, and open writs on Work once it has been looked at
Notice Board: Notices shows town and server news first, then players' notes
Court Writs: Work shows "Court writs today" at the top instead of under the last card
Market: views are grouped: Buy (Materials, Crafted, Auctions, Goods), Sell (Orders, My listings), then History
Market: silver is shown at the top, and listings have column names
Market: the Weavers' and Apothecaries' counters are folded under one "Suppliers" line
